description.en: The effect of Torah study.

*Adam Kadmon* is the first and innermost world, which precedes the four worlds of [*Atzilut*](/topics/atzilut) ([Emanation](/topics/atzilut)), [*Beria*](/topics/beria1) ([Creation](/topics/beria1)), [*Yetzira*](/topics/yetzira1) ([Formation](/topics/yetzira1)), and [*Asiya*](/topics/asiya2) ([Action](/topics/asiya2)). It incorporates all of existence, from its head, that is, the source, which is [*Ein Sof*](/topics/ein-sof1), to its lowest point, which is this physical world. This world is called *Adam Kadmon* because it is depicted in kabbalistic writings in the form of a man, having a head, body and appendages. Although all the worlds are likewise described in the form of a man, this world is the primeval one, before which there is no world, while the other worlds, which are external to it, are “mapped onto it,” lower manifestations of that primeval world: *Atzilut*, from the chest and below to the navel; and *Beria*, *Yetzira*, and *Asiya*, from the navel and below. This world corresponds to the [*sefira*](/topics/sefira2) of [*Keter*](/topics/keter1). Just as [*Keter*](/topics/keter1) itself is often regarded as above the [*sefirot*](/topics/sefirot), so too the world of *Adam Kadmon* is sometimes not considered part of the four worlds.
The [brains](/topics/brains2) of [*Abba*](/topics/abba1), that is, the illumination of [*Ḥokhma*](/topics/hokhma1), are called maturity (*Talmud Eser Sefirot*, v. 7, Q & A 31).

Although challah today is simply known as the braided loaf of bread eaten on Shabbat and Jewish holidays, its origins are in the biblical commandment to separate a portion of dough — known as challah — that would then be given to the priest (kohen).
description.he: אף שבימינו המילה חלה מתארת לחם קלוע הנאכל בשבתות ובחגים, מקורה הוא במצוות התורה להפרשת חלה – נטילת חתיכה מהבצק והקדשתה לכוהן.

description.en: The lowest of the four worlds (planes, or [levels](/topics/level) of reality), the world of *Asiya* parallels the [*sefira*](/topics/sefira2) of [*Malkhut*](/topics/malkhut1). Accordingly, it is also correlated with the “fourth [level](/topics/level)” of a given structure of reality, like [*Malkhut*](/topics/malkhut1), which is the fourth [level](/topics/level) of the five main [*sefirot*](/topics/sefirot) ([*Keter*](/topics/keter1) is the root [level](/topics/level), followed by the next four, hence, the final [*sefira*](/topics/sefira2) of [*Malkhut*](/topics/malkhut1) is considered “fourth,” as is the plane of *Asiya*). It is called *Asiya*, or “Actualization,” because it is where all the wills and forces that descend from the worlds above it are actualized (*na’asim*), or materialized, within it. The lowest [level](/topics/level) of the world of *Asiya* is our material world that we refer to as “this world.” The spiritual entities that exist in the world of *Asiya* are called *ofanim*, which are the spiritual roots of all that exists in the physical reality of this world.
description.he: העולם התחתון מבין ארבעת העולמות, המשתלשלים זה מזה בתהליך הבריאה. הוא נקרא בשם "עשיה" מפני שבו נעשים ויוצאים בפועל כל הרצונות והכוחות שיש בעולמות שמעליו . הדרגה התחתונה של עולם העשיה היא העולם הגשמי שלנו, <<עולם הזה>>. עולם העשיה מקביל בעניינו לספירת ה<<מלכות>> או ל<<בחינה ד'>>. הישויות של עולם העשיה נקראות "אופנים", מעין מלאכים בדרגה נמוכה, שהם השורשים הרוחניים של כל הנמצא בעולם הזה.

description.en: In the Torah, the land of Israel  is described as rife with produce and resources, a land where following God’s commandments is rewarded and flaunting them can cause expulsion. Unlike Egypt, biblical Israel was a land almost entirely dependent on rain, and the Israelites would be more dependent on God when living there. Poets and scholars have long yearned to be in the land of Israel, and its merits and holiness have been extolled across many genres.

description.en: Nighttime serves as the setting for pivotal moments in biblical history, including God’s [covenant of the pieces](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.15.12?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) with Abraham, Jacob’s [wrestling](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.32.23?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) with the angel, the [plague](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus.12.29?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) of the firstborn, and the [splitting of the sea](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus.14.20?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en). Rabbinic sources emphasize the special value of Torah study at night, teaching that a “[thread of kindness](https://www.sefaria.org/Chagigah.12b.8?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en)” accompanies those who engage in it, and many communities observe the custom of studying Torah throughout the night of Shavuot. Sources of Jewish thought and liturgy also portray the night as a particularly fitting time for introspection, devotion, prayer, and revelation.

description.en: The morning prayer service in Judaism—*Shacharit* in Hebrew—consists of four main sections: preparatory prayers and readings; the [Shema](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/shema?tab=admin) and its blessings; the [Amidah](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/shemoneh-esrei?sort=Relevance&tab=admin); and the concluding sections. The Torah is read on Mondays, Thursdays, and Shabbat, as well as on most other special days. Rabbinic sources delve into the origins and significance of daily morning prayers.

description.en: The four species are four plants associated with the holiday of Sukkot. The commandment to gather the four species originates in Leviticus 23:40. Rabbinic sources discuss the exact meaning of each of the phrases in the verse and ultimately identify the four species as: the etrog (citron fruit), lulav (closed frond of a palm tree), hadas (myrtle bough) and aravah (willow branch).

Later Jewish texts describe the importance of recognizing hunger experienced by other people and discuss the obligation of charitably feeding the hungry.

enBio.value: Yosef Karo, expelled from Spain as a child, was a rabbi, Talmudist, mystic and the pre-emiment halachic codifier. His best-known work, the Shulchan Aruch, was accepted in his lifetime and formally recognized thereafter as the definitive statement of Jewish legal and religious practice. He also wrote basic commentaries on the Mishneh Torah and the Arba'ah Turim (the latter forming the basis from which the Shulchan Aruch was distilled). He was also a mystic who received heavenly revelations. Some of these were set down in writing and formed the impetus to come to the Land of Israel. There, he lived in Tsfat, where he took a central role in the attempt by his teacher, Rabbi Yaakov Berav, to revive traditional rabbinic Semikhah.

description.en: Joseph Karo, expelled from Spain as a child, was a rabbi, talmudist, mystic, and preemiment halakhic codifier. His best-known work, the Shulchan Arukh, was accepted in his lifetime and formally recognized thereafter as the definitive statement of Jewish legal and religious practice. He also wrote basic commentaries on Rambam's Mishneh Torah and Jacob ben Ashe's Arba'ah Turim, both of which were major sources for his own Shulchan Arukh. As a mystic, he also received heavenly revelations. Some of these were set down in writing and contributed to his decision to migrate to the land of Israel. There, he lived in Safed, where he supported the effort of his teacher, Rabbi Yaakov Berav, to revive traditional rabbinic ordination (Hebrew: semikhah).

description.en: *Adam Kadmon* is the first and innermost world, which precedes the four worlds of [*Atzilut*](/topics/atzilut) ([Emanation](/topics/atzilut)), [*Beria*](/topics/beria1) ([Creation](/topics/beria1)), [*Yetzira*](/topics/yetzira1) ([Formation](/topics/yetzira1)), and [*Asiya*](/topics/asiya2) ([Action](/topics/asiya2)). It incorporates all of existence, from its head, that is, the source, which is [*Ein Sof*](/topics/ein-sof1), to its lowest point, which is this physical world. This world is called *Adam Kadmon* because it is depicted in kabbalistic writings in the form of a man, having a head, body and appendages. Although all the worlds are likewise described in the form of a man, this world is the primeval one, before which there is no world, while the other worlds, which are external to it, are “mapped onto it,” lower manifestations of that primeval world: *Atzilut*, from the chest and below to the navel; and *Beria*, *Yetzira*, and *Asiya*, from the navel and below. This world corresponds to the [*sefira*](/topics/sefira2) of [*Keter*](/topics/keter1). Just as [*Keter*](/topics/keter1) itself is often regarded as above the [*sefirot*](/topics/sefirot), so too the world of *Adam Kadmon* is sometimes not considered part of the four worlds.

description.en: Meribah is a place mentioned in the books of Exodus and Numbers. In one story in Exodus, the Israelites complain about a lack of water. God instructs Moses to hit a rock; Moses does, and water comes out. The place is then called Massah and Meribah, commemorating the incident. In a similar story described in Numbers, God instructs Moses to take his staff and talk to a rock after the Israelites complain about a lack of water. Moses hits the rock twice and water comes out. God then tells Moses and Aaron that they will not enter Israel, and refers to the water as "water of Meribah."

description.en: Treating strangers well is a fundamental tenet of the Torah, stemming from a communal memory of what it was like to be strangers in the land of Egypt. description.en: “Love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18) is the basis for a central principle known as the Golden Rule, or the concept of treating others as one wants to be treated themselves. Much commentary has been penned attempting to understand the verse’s moral message, scope, practical implications, and role in Judaism.
description.he: "ואהבת לרעך כמוך" - מילים שמגיעים מויקרא יט:יח -  הוא אחד העקרונות הידועים והמרכזיים ביהדות אשר מדגיש את חשיבות ההתייחסות לזולת באדיבות, בכבוד ובאמפתיה. הרעיון מאחורי "ואהבת לרעך כמוך" הוא שעלינו לשאוף להתייחס לאחרים כפי שהיינו רוצים שיתייחסו אלינו, באהבה, בחמלה ובהבנה. מושג זה משתקף גם במסורות דתות ומוסריות אחרות, ולעתים קרובות הוא מצוטט כעיקרון מנחה לקידום הרמוניה חברתית, שיתוף פעולה ושיח בין-דתי.

description.en: This is the name for the first and lowest of the five [levels](/topics/level) (and corresponding lights) of the soul, *nefesh*, [*ruaḥ*](/topics/ruah1), [*neshama*](/topics/neshama2), [*ḥaya*](/topics/haya1), and [*yeḥida*](/topics/yehida1). These five [levels](/topics/level) of the soul correspond to the five primary *sefirot*, of [*Keter*](/topics/keter1), [*Ḥokhma*](/topics/hokhma1), [*Bina*](/topics/bina3), [*Tiferet*](/topics/tiferet1), and [*Malkhut*](/topics/malkhut1), as well as the five worlds, [*Adam Kadmon*](/topics/adam-kadmon2), [*Atzilut*](/topics/atzilut), [*Beria*](/topics/beria1), [*Yetzira*](/topics/yetzira1), and [*Asiya*](/topics/asiya2). The concept of the five [levels](/topics/level) of the soul relates to five qualities of supernal light which illuminate people as well as the [levels](/topics/level) of broader reality. The *nefesh* corresponds to and is the light that belongs to the [*sefira*](/topics/sefira2) of [*Malkhut*](/topics/malkhut1) and the world of [*Asiya*](/topics/asiya2), and it is the first aspect of the soul that is illuminated within a person or an aspect of reality.

The second constriction occurred in one of the formative stages of the [*partzufim*](/topics/partzuf) of [*Adam Kadmon*](/topics/adam-kadmon2) , in order to enable the creation of man and this world. The fourth [level](/topics/level), or phase of creation, which constitutes the will to receive, or the attribute of judgment, also known as the [level](/topics/level) of [*Malkhut*](/topics/malkhut1), rose and mingled with the second [level](/topics/level), which constitutes the will to give, or the attribute of mercy, also known as the [level](/topics/level) of [*Bina*](/topics/bina3), and thus the [partition](/topics/partition2) that is upon the [level](/topics/level) [*Malkhut*](/topics/malkhut1) rose to the second [level](/topics/level) as well. As a consequence of the [partition](/topics/partition2)’s new position, the light of the [levels](/topics/level) beneath the second [level](/topics/level), the third and fourth [levels](/topics/level), was darkened. It is this intermingling of the will to give with the will to receive that creates the capacity for free choice between these options for human beings.

The [book of Ruth](https://www.sefaria.org/Ruth.1?lang=bi) is one of the five megillot (scrolls) found in the section of the Hebrew Bible called Writings and is traditionally read on the holiday of Shavuot. It tells the story of [Ruth](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/ruth?tab=sources), a widow of Moabite origin, who insists on staying with her widowed, Israelite mother-in-law, declaring “Wherever you go, I will go... your people shall be my people, and your God my God” (1:16). Ruth’s loyalty leads her to the field of her kinsman, Boaz, whom she ultimately marries. Together they have a child, who later becomes the grandfather of King David.
description.he: מגילת רות היא השנייה בקובץ חמש מגילות שבחטיבת הכתובים שבמקרא, ונקראת בחג השבועות. היא מספרת את סיפורה של רות, אלמנה שמוצאה במואב, הדבקה בחמותה האלמנה היהודייה ומצהירה "באשר תלכי אלך, עמך עמי ואלוקייך אלוקיי" (רות א, טז). נאמנותה של רות מוליכה אותה לשדהו של מיטיבה בועז, והוא נושא אותה לאישה. בנם הנולד להם נעשה לימים סבו של דוד המלך.

description.en: *Tikkun* means “repair” or “mend.” It is used alongside the word *olam* (world) to express the Jewish responsibility to [repair the world](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/tikkun-olam?sort=Relevance&tab=notable-sources). *Tikkun* can also refer to specific texts read on various occasions, specific nights of Torah study, such as [Hoshanah Rabbah](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/hoshana-rabbah?tab=admin) and [Shavuot](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/shavuot?tab=admin), the process of making a shared courtyard into a personal space so that one can carry in it on Shabbat, or the process of improving [character traits](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/middot?tab=admin).

enBio.value: Nachman of Breslov was one of the most creative chassidic masters, whose thought and teachings continue to resonate within wide circles far beyond his immediate followers. He was a great-grandson of the founder of Chassidut, R. Yisrael Ba'al Shem Tov, and a grandson of another early chassidic master, R. Nachman of Horodenka. Among his many works are a profound presentation of his chassidic and mystical teaching, Likkutei Moharan, and a compilation of his intricate and powerfully evocative stories, Sippurei Ma'asiyot.  Another work relates the events of his transformative journey to and from the Land of Israel. He was severely criticized by certain contemporary chassidic masters, but defended by the leading chassidic master, R. Levi Yitzchak of Berdichev. He moved to Uman less than a year before he passed away from tuberculosis, and his grave there is a pilgrimage site for thousands to this day.

heBio.value: נחמן מברסלב היה אחד ממנהיגי החסידות היצירתיים ביותר, ומחשבתו ותורתו ממשיכים להדהד בחוגים הנמצאים הרבה מעבר לממשיכיו המיידיים. היה נינו של מייסד החסידות, רבי ישראל בעל שם טוב, ונכדו של רבי נחמן מהורודנקה. בין חיבוריו הרבים אפשר למצוא את החיבור המציג את רעיונותיו החסידיים והמיסטיים, ליקוטי מוהר"ן, ואוסף של סיפורים עמוקים ורבי עצמה, סיפורי מעשיות. חיבור נוסף מתאר את האירועים במסעו הטרנספורמטיבי לארץ ישראל וממנה. הוא ספג ביקורת קשה מצד ממנהיגים חסידיים מסוימים בדורו, אך רבי לוי יצחק מברדיצ'ב הגן עליו. רבי נחמן עבר לאומן פחות משנה לפני שנפטר ממחלת השחפת, וקברו משמש אתר עלייה לרגל בעבור אלפים, עד עצם היום הזה.

description.en: Rebbe Nachman of Breslov was one of the most creative Chasidic masters, whose thought and teachings continue to resonate far beyond his immediate followers. He was a great-grandson of the founder of Chasidut, [Rabbi Yisrael Ba'al Shem Tov](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/baal-shem-tov?tab=popular-writing-of), and a grandson of another early Chasidic master, Rabbi Nachman of Horodenka. Among his many works are a profound presentation of his Chasidic and mystical teaching, Likkutei Moharan, and a compilation of his intricate and powerfully evocative stories, Sippurei Ma'asiyot. Another work relates the events of his transformative journey to and from the land of Israel. He was severely criticized by certain contemporary Chasidic masters but was defended by the leading Chasidic master, [Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/levi-yitzchak-of-berditchev). He moved to Uman less than a year before he passed away from tuberculosis, and his grave there is a pilgrimage site to this day.

description.en: Yefet, known as Japheth in English, is a biblical character first mentioned in Genesis 6:10, where he is listed as the third of Noah’s three sons. Together with his brother Shem, he covers his father’s nakedness when Noah gets drunk after emerging from the ark. For this, Noah blesses him. He is described as having seven sons, among them Yavan, considered to be the father of the Greeks.

description.en: Hatred is a concept that appears throughout the Jewish textual tradition. The Torah commands against harboring hatred for one’s fellow in one’s heart, and rabbinic sources discuss the parameters of hatred, under what circumstances hatred might be permitted or even encouraged, how to avoid harboring hatred, and the halakhic ramifications for one whose actions are motivated by hate.

description.en: Hatarat Nedarim (the annulment of vows) is a legal process which allows one to cancel a vow by reciting a text in the presence of three people. It is customary to perform hatarat nedarim in the days leading up to [Rosh HaShanah](https://www.sefaria.org/Rosh_Hashanah?tab=contents) or [Yom Kippur](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/yom-kippur?sort=Relevance&tab=sources), in a version of the ceremony that involves cancelling all vows taken in the past and to be taken in the future.

description.en: Exodus 32 describes the moment when the people of Israel abandon hope that Moses will return from Mount Sinai and turn to Aaron to forge a golden calf to worship. Commentaries across genres discuss the responsibility Aaron bears for this paradigmatic sin, delving into his motivations and deliberations. In many of these commentaries, Aaron's later role as high priest is connected to this moment, as are the specifications for the sin offering.

description.en: The opening chapter of the Torah describes how God created humanity [in the image of God](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.1.27?lang=he&with=all&lang2=en), a concept that fuels the idea that people are to be treated with dignity and respect. The value of human dignity stands behind many Jewish commandments and customs, such as the obligation to [return a cloak](https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.24.13?lang=he&with=all&lang2=en) taken as collateral from a poor person as the night approaches, the duty to promptly [bury the dead](https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.21.23?ven=english|The_Koren_Jerusalem_Bible&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en), and the commandment to respect the elderly. Rabbinic [sources](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.19b.2?lang=he&with=all&lang2=en) discuss situations in which human dignity can override other commandments, mystical texts explore the concept of developing one's inner spark, and ethical books expand upon ways to cultivate the trait of respect for others.

description.en: Sadness is a central part of the human experience. Biblical narratives include sadness as motivating biblical figures — even God. Halakhic texts limit when it is acceptable to be sad and dictate when one must be. Other texts include psychological insights, self-help advice,  and prayers and meditations for help to overcome the pain.
description.he: עצב הוא חלק מרכזי מהחוויה האנושית. בפסוקי התנ"ך עצב משמש לעתים כמניע דמויות מקראיות - אפילו עבור אלוהים. מקורות הלכתיים מגבילים מתי מקובל להיות עצוב ומכתיבים מתי חייבים להיות. מקורות אחרים כוללים תובנות פסיכולוגיות, עצות לעזרה עצמית, תפילות ודרכים נוספות לעזרה כדי להתגבר על הכאב.

description.en: “Gog and Magog” refers to enemies of the Jewish people. Jewish texts describe how, at the dawn of a messianic era, Gog and Magog will wage war against Israel, and God will miraculously defeat them. The terms Gog and Magog first appear together in [Ezekiel 38–39](https://www.sefaria.org/Ezekiel.38.2?ven=Tanakh:_The_Holy_Scriptures,_published_by_JPS&lang=he&with=all&lang2=he), where Gog is the name of a leader, and Magog is his land. In rabbinic literature, Gog and Magog are understood to be the names of two nations or one nation with two names.

The Torah [prohibits](https://www.sefaria.org/Leviticus.19.18?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) taking personal revenge, but also instructs taking revenge against the [Midianites](https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.31.2?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) and notes that [vengeance belongs to God](https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.32.35?lang=bi&with=Rashi&lang2=en). The biblical concept of cities of refuge is designed to protect those who killed accidentally from blood avengers, but the instinct of a [blood avenger](https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.35.27?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) seems to be recognized as natural. In discussing these cases and others, biblical commentators, rabbinic texts, and ethical books throughout the ages grapple with the parameters and role of revenge in Judaism — when it has a place, when it doesn’t, and how to understand sources that provide differing messages.

description.en: The Jewish calendar is a lunarsolar calendar, incorporating elements of a lunar and solar calendar. Sources throughout the Jewish textual tradition discuss the development, significance, and legal aspects of the calendar.

description.en: The bringing forth of something into existence ex nihilo, [*yesh* *me*’*ayin*](/topics/yesh-meayin), is known as *Beria* (Creation). Since the [opacity](/topics/opacity) ([*ovyut*](/topics/ovyut)) in the vessels cannot be revealed in the world of [*Atzilut*](/topics/atzilut) ([Emanation](/topics/atzilut)), but only from the ground of the world of [*Atzilut*](/topics/atzilut) ([Emanation](/topics/atzilut)) and below, it is therefore called *Beria* from that point and below, after the [opacity](/topics/opacity) ([*ovyut*](/topics/ovyut)) that has been revealed. For the [opacity](/topics/opacity) ([*ovyut*](/topics/ovyut)), which is comprised of the [will to receive](/topics/will-to-receive) in the created being, is a form of [*yesh* *me*’*ayin*](/topics/yesh-meayin), creation from nothing. Everything that exists is drawn from God as *yesh miyesh*, literally “something from something,” because there is nothing He does not have, apart from a “will of receiving,” which of necessity He does not possess, since there is no one from whom He could receive, God forbid. This must be understood.

Often translated as bounty, flow, or abundance, *shefa* comes from the Hebrew word *hashpa’a*, which in this context means to give. Rays of sunlight, for example, can be described as the sun’s *shefa*. The rays constitute a “flow” of light from the sun that provides light and sustenance to the earth in bountiful abundance. In kabbalistic thought, *shefa*  refers to different forms of light that flow from God's essence or from the [*sefirot*](/topics/sefirot) and the like. Additionally, *shefa* can be used to refer both to God’s giving to creation, as well as the giving of created beings to each other.

description.en: *Yibbum* is the Torah-mandated marriage of a widow to the brother of her childless husband. If either party does not want to go through with the marriage, an alternative ceremony called [*chalitzah*](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/halitzah?sort=Relevance&tab=notable-sources) is performed. In most contemporary Jewish communities, *chalitzah* is practiced instead of *yibbum*.

There are two women referred to in Tanakh as "daughter of Pharaoh." The first is the woman who pulled [Moses](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/moses) from the Nile and raised him as her son, in her father's house. According to rabbinic tradition, she converted to Judaism, and her name was Bityah, meaning "daughter of God." The second is a wife of [King Solomon](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/king-solomon).

description.en: The world of *nekudim* is the second of the worlds of [*Adam Kadmon*](/topics/adam-kadmon2). It is called by this name because the spiritual [levels](/topics/level) within it are called *nekudot*, or points. In this context, the *nekuda* refers to [*Malkhut*](/topics/malkhut1), the fourth [level](/topics/level), after the first [constriction](/topics/constriction) ([*tzimtzum*](/topics/tzimtzum1)) occurred. As a result of this constriction, [*Malkhut*](/topics/malkhut1) is only a black point without any light whatsoever.Then,as a result of the [second constriction](/topics/second-constriction) ([*tzimtzum*](/topics/tzimtzum1)), [*Malkhut*](/topics/malkhut1) and the [partition](/topics/partition2) that is upon it became intermingled within all the [*sefirot*](/topics/sefirot) and are then present in all the [*sefirot*](/topics/sefirot). As a result of this intermingling, there are ten *nekudot*, or ten *Malkhuyot* with [partitions](/topics/partition2) because the [level](/topics/level) of [*Malkhut*](/topics/malkhut1) with its [partition](/topics/partition2) is present in each of the ten [*sefirot*](/topics/sefirot). This contrasts with the preceding worlds, in which there was only one [*Malkhut*](/topics/malkhut1) and one [partition](/topics/partition2). The world of *nekudim* is also called the “world of breaking,” or the “world of chaos,” because the shattering of the vessels occurred in this world.

Elisha ben Abuyah was a tannaitic sage who adopted a heretical worldview. He is mentioned twice in tannaitic literature and appears in several stories throughout the Talmud and midrashic literature. Elisha is often referred to as “acher” (“other one”) as a result of his heresy.

description.en: Rabban Gamliel (II) was a tannaitic sage in the first and second centuries CE. Rabban Gamliel occasionally acted in ways that involved publicly shaming other rabbis, which led to pushback and his temporary deposition.

description.en: The destruction of the Temple can refer to the destruction of either of the two Temples that stood in Jerusalem in the ancient period. The First Temple, built by King Solomon, was destroyed in 586 BCE by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. The Second Temple, built 70 years after the destruction of the first, was destroyed in 70 CE by the Roman empire. The fast day of Tisha B'Av commemorates the destruction of both Temples, among other historical tragedies.

Consumption of alcoholic beverages and drunkenness are discussed from the first book of the Torah, as Noah plants a vineyard upon leaving his ark and deals with the consequences of his subsequent drunkenness. Other biblical texts convey mixed messages about alcohol: while the book of Psalms extols wine as "[gladdening the human heart](https://www.sefaria.org/Psalms.104.15?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en)," the book of Proverbs warns that "[in the end, [wine] bites like a snake.](https://www.sefaria.org/Proverbs.23.32?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en)" Later stories, legal discussions, and philosophical discourses throughout the Jewish textual tradition take up the topic of alcohol consumption, its role and contributions to Jewish ritual, and its limits and hazards.

description.en: Milk features throughout Jewish texts as a [marker of blessing](https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.26.9?lang=bi&with=Ramban&lang2=en), a legal category, and a metaphor for spiritual sustenance. The biblical prohibition against boiling a goat in its mother's milk becomes the basis for the extensive system of separating meat and dairy in halakhah. Milk also appears in symbolic and poetic contexts, such as in [Song of Songs 4:11](https://www.sefaria.org/Song_of_Songs.4.11?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en), where it represents sweetness and intimacy, and in rabbinic literature [comparing](https://www.sefaria.org/Shir_HaShirim_Rabbah.4.5.1?lang=bi&with=Navigation&lang2=en) Torah to nourishing milk. Many Jews have a [custom](https://www.sefaria.org/Shulchan_Arukh%2C_Orach_Chayim.494.3?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) to consume milk or dairy products on the holiday of Shavuot.

description.en: The twelve spies feature in the books of Numbers and Deuteronomy. They were a group of leaders - one from each tribe - sent by Moses to scout the land of Canaan ahead of the Israelites arrival there. They came back reporting that the land was good, but that it was filled with giants and fearsome enemies. This prompted the Israelites to cry and complain that they did not want to enter the land. Two of the twelve spies, Joshua and Caleb, attempted to assuage their fears and remind the people of God’s commitment that the Israelites’ would enter the land.

description.en: “The Four Children” refers to a rabbinic text incorporated into the *maggid* section of many [haggadahs](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/haggadah?tab=sources). Each child is given a unique answer, built by weaving together different biblical verses. Variations of the text abound.

enBio.value: Onkelos, according to tradition, was a Roman convert to Judaism who lived in the first or second century. He translated Tanach into Aramaic, the spoken language of the day. Some identify Onkelos with a convert named Aquilas who translated the Tanach into Greek. According to tradition, he was counseled by his uncle, the emperor, to succeed by buying low and selling high. He later explained his conversion to his incensed uncle by repeating to him his own advice from years past. Onkelos' translation became the standard Aramaic translation, used daily by Jews world-wide long after Aramaic ceased being a living language for most Jews.

heBio.value: אונקלוס, על פי המסורת, היה גר רומאי שחי במאה הראשונה או השנייה לספירה. הוא תרגם את התנ"ך לארמית, השפה המדוברת של אותם ימים. יש המזהים אונקלוס עם עקילס, גר שתרגם את התנ"ך ליוונית. לפי המסורת, לימד אותו דודו הקיסר שכדי להצליח צריך לקנות בזול ולמכור ביקר. מאוחר יותר הסביר את גיורו לדודו  המרוגז לפי אותה עצה שדודו נתן לו. תרגומו של אונקלוס נהיה התרגום הארמי הסטנדרטי הנדפס בכל החומשים, ויהודים מכל רחבי העולם משתמשים בו, הרבה זמן אחרי שארמית חדלה מלהיות שפה חיה.

description.en: As a powerful emotion and a universal part of the human experience, grief appears throughout the Jewish textual tradition. Biblical and talmudic sources tell stories of people who grieve, halakhic texts discuss practices and customs of mourning, and works of Jewish thought discuss how to process and cope with grief.

The *yod* of *Havaya* is the first expansion of the [light](/topics/light2), which is called the first level (see v. 1, Answers, answer 69). The first *heh* of *Havaya* is the first prevailment in the [light](/topics/light2), called the second level. The *vav* of *Havaya* is the second expansion of the [light](/topics/light2), which is called the third level. Finally, the last *heh* of *Havaya* is the second prevailment in the [light](/topics/light2), called the fourth level (*Talmud Eser Sefirot*, v. 1, Q & A 70).

Although the supernal light wishes to permeate every [level](/topics/level) of reality, reality cannot fully contain it on account of its limited vessels, or receptacles. Therefore the supernal light that cannot be contained, called surrounding light, is always situated in the background and so has an indirect influence on reality. This contrasts with the [inner light](/topics/inner-light1), which is the supernal light that is currently [enclothed](/topics/enclothe) in reality and permeates it in accordance with the reality’s capacity to contain it. When reality is fully rectified in the future, the surrounding light too will be able to permeate it.

Adar is the sixth month of the Hebrew calendar. In seven out of every 19 years, a second month of Adar is added in order to keep the agricultural cycle of the Jewish lunar calendar synchronized with the solar year. [The rabbis taught](https://www.sefaria.org/Taanit.29a.18?vhe=William_Davidson_Edition_-_Vocalized_Aramaic&lang=bi) that one rejoices when the month of Adar begins.

description.en: *Tekhelet* is a special blue or blue-ish dye that the Torah designates for use in ritual fringes, tapestries in the Tabernacle, and clothing of the high priest. Rabbinic literature explains that *tekhelet* is derived from a sea creature called the *chilazon* and delves into the spiritual significance of the dye. At some point in history, *tekhelet* disappeared from ritual practice, likely because the traditions of how to identify the *chilazon* or how to produce *tekhelet* were lost — yet acknowledgement of its spiritual relevance endured, such as the recitation of the commandment to wear *tekhelet* as part of the daily Shema prayer. Since the 19th century, there has been [renewed](https://www.sefaria.org/Treasures_Hidden_in_the_Sand?tab=contents) [discussion](https://www.sefaria.org/Ptil_Tekhelet?tab=contents) among scholars about the identification and usage of *tekhelet* in ritual fringes.

description.en: In modern times, the concept of "*tikkun olam*" — translated as “repair,” “betterment,” or “improvement” of the world — is commonly used to refer to the pursuit of social justice. When the term first appears throughout the [fourth chapter of tractate Gittin](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Gittin.4.1?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) in the Mishnah, it refers to rabbinic edicts likely meant to foster social order, like [Hillel](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/hillel?tab=admin)’s [prozbul](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/prozbul?tab=admin) and the decree that two witnesses [must sign](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Gittin.4.3?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) a divorce document. In the ancient [*Aleinu*](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/aleinu?tab=admin) prayer, the term is used in the context of a future messianic era in which idolatry would be obliterated, and all would recognize God’s omnipotence. In kabbalistic literature, *tikkun olam* means performing religious acts in order to gather fragments of God’s light and return them to their source.

description.en: *Kelippot* are [levels](/topics/level) of reality that do not contain any will to give, only the will to receive. Since their essence is one of receiving or “taking,” they are constantly trying to pull all of reality into themselves – in essence, to swallow everything in existence. Since the essence of life is the divine light, which is composed entirely of the energy of giving, they and all that is connected to them are considered to be “dead.” The *kelippot* are therefore compared to the husks or shells of a fruit, which are detached from the life that is inside the fruit. Since these entities are wholly receiving, unable to give, they have no true connection with the life force of creation, like the dead.

The Hasmonean dynasty was a ruling dynasty in ancient Judea established by the Maccabees, fighters from a priestly Jewish family who successfully waged war against the Seleucid Greeks and rededicated the Second Temple in Jerusalem in 164 BCE. Hasmonean leaders occupied the position of high priest and eventually the kingship as well. The dynasty ruled from 167 BCE to 37 BCE.

description.he: עמון הוא שמה של אומה מצאצאי לוט ששכנה ממזרח לישראל, בירדן של ימינו. בדומה למואב – ואף שלעיתים קרובות היו שתי האומות הללו בסכסוך – קיבלו בני ישראל את אותן ההוראות ביחס לעמון, כלומר לא לתקוף אותם אך גם לא להטמיע אותם בהם.
description.en: Descended from Lot, Ammon was a nation that dwelled east of Israel in present-day Jordan. As with Moab — and although they were frequently in conflict — the Israelites were specifically instructed by the Torah to neither attack nor absorb the Ammonites.

A contemporary of Rabbah, Rav Yosef became the head of the academy in Pumpedita after Rabbah's death. He was known for his humility and for his mastery of the corpus of Jewish law. While wealthy, Rav Yosef had health issues which brought him blindness and the loss of memory.
description.he: רב יוסף היה בן זמנו של רבה ומונה לראשות ישיבת פומבדיתא לאחר מותו. נודע בענוותו ובידע המקיף שלו בהלכה. היה עשיר וסבל מבעיות בריאותיות שגרמו לו לעיוורון ולאובדן זיכרון.

description.en: The Mincha Offering (Korban Mincha) was the daily afternoon sacrifice of fine flour with olive oil and frankincense that was offered upon the Copper Altar in the Mishkan and in the Temple.
description.he: קורבן מנחה הוא קורבן מן הצומח המורכב מקמח מנופה, שמן זית וסולת. המנחה הוקטרה מדי יום אחר הצוהריים על מזבח הנחושת במשכן, ולאחר מכן במקדש.

description.en: In the opening chapter of the Torah, God creates the moon, alongside other celestial bodies, on the fourth day of creation. In Jewish tradition and practice, the moon plays a central role in determining the calendar: New Hebrew months start with the appearance of new moons, which also lead to the determination of holiday dates. Texts throughout the ages discuss the moon's symbolism and significance; halakhic practices related to the moon, like the concept of blessing the new moon; and ways in which the lunar calendar interacts with the solar calendar.

description.en: Zion — in Hebrew, *Tzion* — is another name for Jerusalem in the Bible. It can also refer to the land of Israel. The term often highlights a spiritual connection between heaven and earth or a yearning for messianic redemption.

description.en: Biblical [texts](https://www.sefaria.org/Jeremiah.31.8?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) describe people with disabilities as an organic part of the community. Halakhic texts analyze how certain disabilities can affect the fulfillment of particular commandments, with some rulings being reevaluated in light of modern medical technology and contemporary understandings. Rabbinic literature, with its emphasis on learning, discusses tailoring education to the needs of the pupil, including those with disabilities. Works throughout the Jewish textual tradition explore the concept of disability from a range of perspectives.

Renewal is a concept that can involve revitalizing, reinvigorating, or returning to an original state. In Judaism, the term can be used to refer to a specific 20th-century Jewish movement, but it is also a concept found throughout biblical and rabbinic literature. The idea is particularly prevalent throughout Chasidic texts, which emphasize performing routine commandments as if it were one’s first time performing them.
description.he: התחדשות היא רעיון חזרת המצב לקדמותו לאחר שינוי, או היווספות פרטים ומאפיינים חדשים לדבר קיים. ביהדות, המושג יכול להתייחס לתנועה יהודית ספציפית במאה ה-20 אשר שמה דגש על הרעננות והחיוניות בחוויה האלוהית, או למושג שמופיע רבות בתנ״ך ובספרות חז״ל. ניתן למצוא את רעיון ההתחדשות גם בספרי חסידות רבים המדגישים את חשיבות יישום רעיון זה בקיום המצוות המעשיות.

description.he: המלך ינאי, הידוע גם בשם "אלכסנדר ינאי", היה מלך חשמונאי שהרחיב את גבולות הממלכה היהודית אך זרע זרעים של מלחמה ושל יחס מחפיר לחכמים בני עמו". רק כלפי גיסו, רבי שמעון בן שטח, נהג ינאי באופן אחר ואף מינה אותו ליועץ.
description.en: King Yannai, or Alexander Jannaeus, was a Hasmonean king who expanded the kingdom of Judea but left a legacy of war and terrible treatment of Jewish scholars. The exception to this vicious treatment was his brother-in-law Rabbi Shimon ben Shetach, from whom he received counsel.

The third of the pairs, Yehudah b. Tabbai and Shimon b. Shetach served during the tumultuous reign of Alexander Yannai. Though Yannai's brother-in-law, Shimon had to hide at the height of Yannai's persecution of the Pharisees; while Yehudah fled to Egypt. Nevertheless, Shimon wrested control of the Sanhedrin away from the Sadducees.
description.he: הזוג השלישי, יהודה בן טבאי ושמעון בן שטח, כיהנו בתקופה הסוערת של שלטון אלכסנדר ינאי. אף ששמעון היה גיסו של ינאי, הוא נאלץ להסתתר בשיאה של רדיפת הפרושים על ידי ינאי, ויהודה ברח למצרים. למרות זאת הצליח שמעון להשיג שליטה על הסנהדרין במקום הצדוקים.

description.en: A bar mitzvah is a coming of age ceremony, traditionally marked for Jewish boys at the age of 13. At this age, rabbinic sources indicate that boys become obligated in the commandments and accountable for their own actions. The practice of marking this transition with a religious ceremony can be traced back to the medieval period.
description.he: בר מצווה (בארמית: בן מצווה) הוא נער יהודי שנעשה מחוייב בקיום מצוות בהגיעו לגיל 13. 'בר מצווה' הוא גם שמו של טקס המעבר שמציין את קבלת קיום המצוות. מסורות טקס שונות התגבשו במהלך הדורות, ביניהן בולט המנהג בו הנער קורא בתורה ואביו מברך "ברוך שפטרני מעונשו של זה".

description.he: במקורות רבים בספרות היהודית, הפוריות, בין אם של אדמה ובין אם של אישה,  נתפסת כברכה מן האל. ברכות מקראיות ותפילות חז"ליות מרבות לבקש את חסדו של האל להענקת שפע, חיים ופרי בטן. סיפורים רבים במקרא ובספרות חז"ל עוסקים במשפחות שנאבקו בעקרות, ובאל ש"פותח רחם", ומאפשר את לידת הדורות הבאים.

description.en: The candelabra used to fulfill the mitzvah of lighting Chanukkah candles is called a *chanukkiah.* Sometimes also called a menorah, it is lit in homes and synagogues during Chanukkah to commemorate the miracle of the holiday, in which one day's worth of oil for the Temple [menorah](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/menorah1?tab=admin) burned for eight days. A chanukkiah has a spot for a candle for each of the eight nights and an additional one for the *shamash,* the candle used to light the others.

description.en: Tamar was Judah's daughter-in-law. After she married two of his sons who then died, he refused to do his duty by giving her his third son in marriage. Instead, she seduced him by pretending to be a prostitute. She kept his personal effects as a pledge and used them to prove that he owed her his household and protection. The son they had became an ancestor of King David.

description.en: Ezekiel was a prophet who spoke from Babylonian exile during the destruction of the First Temple. He had visions about [God's chariot](https://www.sefaria.org/Ezekiel.1.3?ven=Tanakh:_The_Holy_Scriptures,_published_by_JPS&lang=he&with=all&lang2=he), dry [bones](https://www.sefaria.org/Ezekiel.37.1?ven=Tanakh:_The_Holy_Scriptures,_published_by_JPS&lang=he&with=all&lang2=he) coming to life, a [future Temple](https://www.sefaria.org/Ezekiel.40.1?ven=Tanakh:_The_Holy_Scriptures,_published_by_JPS&lang=he&with=all&lang2=he), and more. According to Jewish tradition, accounts of his visions make up the [book of Ezekiel](https://www.sefaria.org/Ezekiel?tab=contents).

description.en:
Many biblical characters express thankfulness and laughter; the first character described explicitly as feeling happy is [Aaron](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus.4.14?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en). Later parts of the Torah tell of the [happiness](https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.14.26?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) that will accompany worshiping God in God’s chosen place in the land of Israel, and the Torah commands [rejoicing](https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.16.14?lang=bi&aliyot=0) on the festivals.
Some Jewish thinkers see happiness as naturally accompanying, or as something that should accompany, [performing the commandments](https://www.sefaria.org.il/Mishneh_Torah%2C_Shofar%2C_Sukkah_and_Lulav.8.15?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en), and as an inherent part of fulfilling them. Others minimize the role that happiness ought to play. Jewish wisdom texts offer ideas about how one can arrive at true happiness, like by being [content with what one has](https://www.sefaria.org/Pirkei_Avot.4.1?ven=hebrew|Torat_Emet_357&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en).

description.en: Comfort appears in the Jewish tradition as an ease to be wished and prayed for, as a luxury to be wary of, and as an assistance to be offered to others. The act of comforting those in grief or distress in particular is a personal and communal obligation, and also a divine act. Halakhah (Jewish law) regulating mourning practices provides guidelines for mourners and their supporters receiving and giving comfort after the death of a close family member. In the Tanakh (Hebrew Bible), prophets such as Isaiah and Jeremiah preach prophecies of comfort in response to national catastrophes (as well as prophecies of rebuke and warning in advance of them). Certain such prophecies of consolation from the book of Isaiah are traditionally read publicly in the seven weeks following the communal mourning day of Tisha B’Av.

description.en: The priestly service consisted of ritual worship carried out by priests in the [Tabernacle (Mishkan)](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/mishkan?tab=sources) and later in the Temple. The service included offering daily sacrifices, cleaning and preparing the altar for sacrifice, arranging the [menorah](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/menorah1?tab=sources) for lighting, offering the [ketoret](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/incense?tab=sources), and more. Particulars of the service are discussed in detail in the [book of Leviticus](https://www.sefaria.org/Leviticus?tab=contents) and in the fifth order of the Mishnah and Talmud, [Kodashim](https://www.sefaria.org/texts/Mishnah/Seder%20Kodashim).

While the book of Proverbs [declares](https://www.sefaria.org/Proverbs.31.30?lang=en) that "beauty is vain" and only "fear of God" is praiseworthy, the Torah notes the beauty of many of its central characters – like Sarah, Rachel, and Joseph, to name a few. Biblical commentators, rabbinic literature, and works of musar and Jewish thought all reckon with the role beauty – physical beauty, spiritual beauty, the beauty of human and animal forms, beauty of the Temple, and more – plays in Judaism, analyzing when it is to be seen as a value to strive for and when it is to be dismissed as a frivolous distraction from more important matters.

The commandment to gather the four species originates in [Leviticus 23:40](https://www.sefaria.org/Leviticus.23.40?lang=he&with=Translations&lang2=he); rabbinic sources discuss the exact meaning of each of the phrases in the verse and ultimately identify "the product of *hadar*  trees" as the etrog.

description.en: Shifrah and Puah are biblical characters mentioned in [Exodus 1](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus.1.15?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en). They are described as midwives who defy Pharaoh’s orders to kill all Israelite baby boys. Instead, Shifrah and Puah keep the babies alive, telling Pharaoh that the Israelite women give birth before the midwives are able to get there. God rewards the midwives for their actions. The midrash identifies Shifrah and Puah as [Yokheved](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/yokheved) and her daughter [Miriam](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/miriam), respectively.

description.en: Kaddish is an Aramaic prayer that declares praise of God. Its four main variants punctuate Jewish prayer services, marking the end of each section and its conclusion. It describes God's holiness and greatness and calls for the recognition of God's eternal rule over all of mankind. It is only recited in the presence of a prayer quorum and is further adapted for different contexts, including burials and to mark ritually the conclusion of a significant body of learning, a siyyum.

description.en: The tree of knowledge is a tree that features in the opening chapters of the [book of Genesis](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis?tab=contents). God causes the tree to grow in the [Garden of Eden](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/garden-of-eden?tab=sources), and commands [Adam](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/adam?tab=sources) not to eat from it, lest he die. In the following chapter, [Eve](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/eve?tab=sources), following the enticing of a snake, notices the desirable qualities of a tree in the Garden. She eats from the tree's fruits and gives to Adam as well. God then calls out to Adam, and describes consequences that the snake, Eve, and Adam will each face as a result of their actions.

This is the [light](/topics/light2) that is not received in the fourth level. That is, its special function is to fill the fourth level, which, however, does not receive the [light](/topics/light2), on account of the [partition](/topics/partition2) that blocks and rebuffs it. This action is called [fusion through collision](/topics/fusion-through-collision) (see *Histaklut Penimit*, v. 2, section 22, s.v., “*ve-hineh*”). Likewise, every receiving [vessel](/topics/vessel1) in the [*partzufim*](/topics/partzuf), from the [constriction](/topics/constriction) ([*tzimtzum*](/topics/tzimtzum1)) and onwards, is drawn from this returning light, which serves for them in place of the fourth level in [*Ein Sof*](/topics/ein-sof1).

The concept of souls being reborn in other bodies or things after death is not explicitly mentioned in the Bible or in classical rabbinic texts like the Mishnah and Talmud but is discussed in later kabbalistic texts and works of Jewish thought. Some of these texts debate the existence of reincarnation, while others explain the purpose of reincarnation, how some biblical figures were reincarnations of other biblical figures, and how certain commandments in the Torah help facilitate the process of reincarnation.

description.en: The mouth, as the lowest organ in the human head, represents the [*sefira*](/topics/sefira2) of [*Malkhut*](/topics/malkhut1), the last and lowest of the [*sefirot*](/topics/sefirot). With respect to the structure of the [*partzuf*](/topics/partzuf1), which corresponds to the entire structure of man, the mouth is the [*Malkhut*](/topics/malkhut1) of the ten *sefirot* of the [head](/topics/head2).
The [*Malkhut*](/topics/malkhut1) of the [head](/topics/head2) is called mouth (*Talmud Eser Sefirot*, v. 3, Q & A 80).

Havdalah — literally, separation — is the ritual that marks the end of Shabbat, separating it from the rest of the week. It consists of blessings over wine, fire, and sweet fragrances, and the separation between holy time and non-holy time, light and darkness, and Israel and the nations.

The first appearance of the phrase "tree of life" (*etz chaim* in Hebrew) in the Torah is in the Genesis story: a tree of life grows in the garden of Eden alongside the tree of knowledge. A [verse](https://www.sefaria.org/Proverbs.3.18?lang=bi) from Proverbs comparing the Torah to a tree of life is commonly sung in Ashkenazi synagogues when returning the Torah to the ark, and the term is used [elsewhere](https://www.sefaria.org/Proverbs.11.30?lang=bi&with=Navigation&lang2=en) [in](https://www.sefaria.org/Proverbs.15.4?lang=bi&with=Navigation&lang2=en) the book of Proverbs as well. In kabbalistic sources, the tree of life often represents a diagram of ten divine emanations, or *sefirot*.* It is also the title of a kabbalistic [book](https://www.sefaria.org/Sefer_Etz_Chaim?tab=contents) by Rabbi Chaim Vital.

description.en: Many biblical and rabbinic sources describe God using the language of physicality, but influential rabbinic texts emphasize that denial of God's physicality is a [key principle of Jewish faith](https://www.sefaria.org/Rambam_on_Mishnah_Sanhedrin.10.1.18?lang=en). Philosophers, scholars, kabbalists, and commentators have all attempted to explain how a transcendent God can be described in human terms. A few have maintained that God does or could indeed possess a physical form, some have interpreted physical language in traditional sources metaphorically, and some have reinterpreted it in light of kabbalistic concepts.

Rivers feature from the opening chapters of the Torah, as the book of Genesis [describes](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.2.10?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) a river that emerges from the garden of Eden and divides into four rivers that water the world. They also play a role in other key biblical narratives: The Nile river [is turned](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus.7.20?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) to blood and serves as the setting for several of the plagues brought upon Egypt, while the Jordan River is [crossed](https://www.sefaria.org/Joshua.3.17?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) by the people of Israel as they enter the land of Israel and helps define the land’s borders. Later Jewish texts explore the halakhic implications of rivers  — such as what types of rivers may be entered on Shabbat — as well as their symbolic and mystical significance.

description.en: Jewish texts often portray human beings as working together with one another and with God to build and sustain the world. The Torah's first description of marriage [acknowledges](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.2.18?lang=bi&aliyot=0) that humans are not meant to be alone, presenting Adam and Eve as counterparts. Later biblical narratives highlight partnerships such as those of Moses and Aaron, who lead the people of Israel together. Rabbinic literature emphasizes the partnership between [study companions](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/chevruta?tab=admin) (*chevrutot*), teaching that Torah is best learned through dialogue and collaboration. Jewish law also recognizes formal business partnerships (*shutafut*), and the Talmud frequently discusses the rights and responsibilities of partners who share property, labor, or profit.

description.en: *Ban*, or *bet-nun*, is the numerical value of 52 in Hebrew letters (*nun*=50; *bet*=2). This numerical value is derived from the letters of the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God referred to as the name of [Havaya](/topics/havaya2), when they are spelled out in full using the letter *heh*. In other words, each of its letters of the name of [Havaya](/topics/havaya2) is written out as a separate word, and the letter *heh* is used in order to fill out the letters, as follows: The *yod* is spelled out as *yod-vav-dalet* (יוד), the *heh* is spelled *heh-heh* (הה), the *vav* is spelled *vav-vav* (וו), and the final *heh* is spelled *heh-heh* (הה). *Ban* represents the [level](/topics/level) of [*Malkhut*](/topics/malkhut1) or the light of [*Malkhut*](/topics/malkhut1).
The light of [Ḥokhma](/topics/hokhma1), in the mystical meaning of the verse (Ecclesiastes 7:12): “Wisdom [*ḥokhma*] preserves the life of he who has it” (*Talmud Eser Sefirot*, v. 2, Q & A 27).

The opening chapter of the Torah [describes](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.1.11?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) how God created plants, trees, and vegetation on the third day of creation. Jewish law includes many commandments related to plants and agriculture, such as leaving the corners of fields for the poor ([*peah*](https://www.sefaria.org/Leviticus.19.9?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en)), observing the sabbatical year ([*shemittah*](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/shemitah?tab=admin)), and refraining from eating a tree's fruit during its first three years ([*orlah*](https://www.sefaria.org/Leviticus.19.23?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en)). The Prophets and works of Jewish thought frequently use plants as metaphors – like in the [comparison](https://www.sefaria.org/Jeremiah.17.8?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) of righteous people to flourishing trees planted by water – and as symbols of life, growth, and God's ongoing care for creation.

Proverbs (“Mishlei”), the second book of the section in the Hebrew Bible called Writings, contains guidance for living a wise, moral, and righteous life, in the form of poems and short statements. It consists of both general observations about human nature as well as lessons directly instructing the listener to take a course of action, covering themes like avoiding bad influences, the value of hard work, properly using the power of speech, and the importance of fearing God.

description.en: Wind plays a role from the very beginning of the Torah, as a [wind from God](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.1.2?lang=bi&vside=The_Contemporary_Torah,_Jewish_Publication_Society,_2006|en&with=Translation%20Open&lang2=en) sweeps over the waters in the opening verses of Genesis. Winds are critical in other prominent biblical stories as well, such as when the wind helps split the Red Sea, brings [quail](https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.11.31?lang=bi&aliyot=0) to the desert, or helps revive the dead in Ezekiel's [Valley of Dry Bones prophecy](https://www.sefaria.org/Ezekiel.37.1?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en). In rabbinic texts, the rabbis discuss how wind affects areas of halakhah, such as under what conditions someone is [liable for damages](https://www.sefaria.org.il/Bava_Kamma.60a.4?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) caused by wind and what types of wind the [sukkah walls](https://www.sefaria.org.il/Sukkah.23a.4?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) must withstand. The word "wind" is also used in the context of the directions north, east, south, and west and their spiritual significance, as well as to refer to a person's [spirit](https://www.sefaria.org.il/Pirkei_Avot.4.4?ven=hebrew|Torat_Emet_357&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) or a moral force.

description.en: The ten [*sefirot*](/topics/sefirot) of the level of [*Malkhut*](/topics/malkhut1), which receives from [*Ze’er Anpin*](/topics/zeer-anpin1), are called the world of *Asiya*.

This is the name for the second of the five [levels](/topics/level) (and corresponding light) of the soul: [*nefesh*](/topics/nefesh), [*ruaḥ*](/topics/ruah1), [*neshama*](/topics/neshama2), [*ḥaya*](/topics/haya1), and [*yeḥida*](/topics/yehida1). These five [levels](/topics/level) of the soul correspond to the five primary *sefirot*, [*Keter*](/topics/keter1), [*Ḥokhma*](/topics/hokhma1), [*Bina*](/topics/bina3), [*Tiferet*](/topics/tiferet1), and [*Malkhut*](/topics/malkhut1), as well as the five worlds, [*Adam Kadmon*](/topics/adam-kadmon2), [*Atzilut*](/topics/atzilut), [*Beria*](/topics/beria1), [*Yetzira*](/topics/yetzira1), and [*Asiya*](/topics/asiya2). The *ruaḥ* [level](/topics/level) of the soul corresponds to and is the light of the [level](/topics/level) of [*Tiferet*](/topics/tiferet1) and the world of [*Yetzira*](/topics/yetzira1). A person attains the illumination of this aspect of the soul after first attaining the illumination of the lowest part, which is the [*nefesh*](/topics/nefesh).

Teaching is a central value in Judaism that features in a variety of context. The biblical patriarch Abraham is instructed to teach his descendants the ways of justice and righteousness, for examples, and rabbinic literature analyzes the responsibilities of parents to ensure that their children receive an education.

description.en: Clouds feature in the Torah in various contexts: God [tells](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.9.14-16?lang=bi&aliyot=0) Noah and his family that a rainbow in a cloud will serve as a sign of God's covenant with humanity and promise to never again to destroy the world with a flood. A [heavy cloud](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus.19.16?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) descends on Mount Sinai as the people of Israel receive the Torah, and a pillar of cloud from God leads the people of Israel as they wander through the desert. Later Jewish texts analyze the meaning of clouds in biblical stories, the mystical significance of clouds, and halakhic (legal) considerations relating to clouds — like how movements of clouds may affect when one says a blessing on lightning or thunder.

description.en: The Bible tells the stories of several rebellions, like that of [Korach](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/korach?sort=Relevance&tab=notable-sources) and his followers, those of [Adoniah](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/adoniah?tab=admin) and [Absalom](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/absalom?tab=admin) against their father, King David, and the anointing of [Jehu](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/yehu?tab=admin) as king as a rebellion against [Ahab](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/ahab?tab=admin). The Torah also discusses how parents deal with [a wayward and rebellious son](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/ben-sorer-umoreh?tab=admin). Post-biblical Jewish history is filled with notable revolts and rebellions, like the [Maccabean](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/maccabees?tab=admin) revolt and the [Bar Kokhba](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/bar-kokhba?tab=admin) revolt.

description.en: The term *neshama* commonly refers to the soul, the divine aspect that exists within every being and sustains it. But according to the teachings of the Kabbala, the soul actually contains five [levels](/topics/level) or lights – [*nefesh*](/topics/nefesh), [*ruaḥ*](/topics/ruah1), [*neshama*](/topics/neshama2), [*ḥaya*](/topics/haya1), and [*yeḥida*](/topics/yehida1) – the third of which is called “*neshama*.” These five [levels](/topics/level) (synonymous with the five lights that correspond and fill the five [*sefirot*](/topics/sefirot) vessels) of the soul correspond to the five [*sefirot*](/topics/sefirot) of [*Keter*](/topics/keter1), [*Ḥokhma*](/topics/hokhma1), [*Bina*](/topics/bina3), [*Tiferet*](/topics/tiferet1), and [*Malkhut*](/topics/malkhut1), as well as the five worlds of [*Adam Kadmon*](/topics/adam-kadmon2), [*Atzilut*](/topics/atzilut), [*Beria*](/topics/beria1), [*Yetzira*](/topics/yetzira1), and [*Asiya*](/topics/asiya2).The *neshama* [level](/topics/level) corresponds to the [*sefira*](/topics/sefira2) of [*Bina*](/topics/bina3) and the world of [*Beria*](/topics/beria1), and represents the light that illuminates this [*sefira*](/topics/sefira2) and world. Therefore one merits it – i.e., it illuminates in the body of a person or a [level](/topics/level) – only after meriting the lower lights (soul [levels](/topics/level)), which are [*nefesh*](/topics/nefesh) and [*ruaḥ*](/topics/ruah1). After attaining it, one can merit the higher lights of [*ḥaya*](/topics/haya1) and [*yeḥida*](/topics/yehida1).

The redemption of captives is a topic discussed throughout rabbinic literature. Instances of redeeming captives are found in the Bible, for example when Abraham [goes to war](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.14.14?ven=The_Koren_Jerusalem_Bible&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) with four kings in order to save his captured nephew, [Lot](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/lot?tab=sources). While sources stress the importance of redeeming captives, calling it a "[great mitzvah](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.8b.2?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en)," other texts warn not to redeem captives [for more than their value](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Gittin.4.6?lang=bi).

description.en: The Torah uses a version of the word "wholeness" in the context of a commandment to have "[completely honest](https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.25.15?lang=bi&with=Translations&lang2=en)" weights and measures and in the context of the commandment to build the altar with [whole stones](https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.27.6?lang=bi&with=Translations&lang2=en). Verses in the Prophets section of the Hebrew Bible speak of [wholeness](https://www.sefaria.org/I_Kings.8.61?lang=bi&with=Translations&lang2=en) of the [heart](https://www.sefaria.org/I_Kings.15.3?lang=bi&with=Translations&lang2=en), meaning honesty and thorough commitment. Sources of Jewish thought use the Hebrew word for "wholeness" – *sheleimut* – to talk about the goal of achieving [spiritual perfection](https://www.sefaria.org/Guide_for_the_Perplexed%2C_Part_1.2.4?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en), discussing different types of wholeness: wholeness of intention, wholeness of heart, [physical](https://www.sefaria.org/Guide_for_the_Perplexed%2C_Part_3.28.1?ven=hebrew|Makbili_Edition,_Mif%27al_Mishneh_Torah,_2024&lang=bi) wholeness, and more.

Paradoxically, the Torah requires Jews to remember [Amalek's](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/amalek?tab=sources) attack [on them as they left slavery in Egypt](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus.17.8?ven=The_Contemporary_Torah,_Jewish_Publication_Society,_2006&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) even as they are required simultaneously to "blot out the memory of Amalek." This mitzvah is typically fulfilled by ensuring that one hears the special liturgical reading of the verses in Deuteronomy that contain this commandment on the Shabbat before the holiday of [Purim](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/purim?tab=sources), which celebrates the Jewish triumph over the wicked Amalekite [Haman](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/jerusalem?sort=Relevance&tab=sources).

description.en: Rest is the abstention from creative work. After the six days of creation, God rested, and the fourth of the Ten Commandments — Shabbat — is to cease from creative work and rest just as God did. The Torah also commands that the land of Israel be left to lie fallow every seventh year in observance of [shemittah](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/shemitah?tab=sources). Rest is also required on holidays. While rest is the means of renewing our bodies and souls, tradition also recognizes it as a taste of the world to come.
description.he: מנוחה היא הימנעות מעבודת יצירה. לאחר ששת ימי הבריאה אלוהים נח, והדיבר הרביעי מבין עשרת הדיברות - שבת - הוא להפסיק מעבודת יצירה ולנוח בדיוק כפי שעשה אלוהים. התורה מצווה גם על השמיטה, שלא לעבוד את ארץ ישראל במשך שנה אחת כל שבע שנים. מנוחה נדרשת גם בחגים. בעוד שמנוחה היא האמצעי לחידוש גופנו ונשמתנו, המסורת מכירה בה גם כטעימה מהעולם הבא.

description.en: In biblical literature, dew appears as a marker of [divine sustenance](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.27.28?lang=bi&aliyot=0) and [blessing](https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.33.13?lang=bi&aliyot=0). Many Jews recite a liturgical [poem](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat_Siddur_Sefard_Linear%2C_Prayers_for_Yom_Tov%2C_Musaf_for_Yom_Tov%2C_Prayer_for_Dew.1?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) called *tefillat tal* — "a prayer for dew" — on the holiday of Passover, and then continue to incorporate a [line](https://www.sefaria.org/Siddur_Edot_HaMizrach%2C_Weekday_Shacharit%2C_Amida.5?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) about dew in the daily Amidah (standing prayer) throughout the spring and summer months. Dew is also discussed in the context of resurrection, as a metaphor for Torah, and in halakhic (legal) discussions about ritual impurity.

description.en: Bezalel is a biblical character who features in the Book of Exodus. He was the artisan charged with building the [mishkan](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/mishkan?tab=sources) (tabernacle), its vessels, and the [priestly garments](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/priestly-garments?tab=sources), assisted by Oholiav and other workers. The Torah describes how God filled Bezalel with ["with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship."](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus.31.3?ven=The_Koren_Jerusalem_Bible&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en)

The opening chapter of the Torah recounts how humanity, from the outset of its creation, is charged with [mastering the natural world](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.1.28?lang=he&with=all&lang2=en). When Adam and Eve sin in the garden of Eden, [God tells Adam](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.3.19?lang=he&with=Translations&lang2=en) that he will now have toil by the sweat of his brow to cultivate the land and produce bread. Later in biblical literature, agriculture becomes the basis of national and religious life as the people of Israel settle in the land of Israel. Many commandments and rituals are centered upon agriculture and the agricultural calendar – like tithing produce for the poor, letting the land rest during the seventh year, and bringing first fruits to the Temple. These and other agricultural topics are the focus of the first order of the Mishnah, [Zeraim](https://www.sefaria.org/texts/Mishnah/Seder%20Zeraim).

description.en: Shabbat HaGadol (“The Great Shabbat”) is the Shabbat that immediately precedes the holiday of Passover. Jewish texts offer many explanations as to why this Shabbat is called “great,” like those that  point to a great miracle performed on this Shabbat during the exodus, or those that point to the word “great” at the end of the haftarah portion traditionally read on this Shabbat. In many communities, the rabbi delivers a lengthy sermon on a Passover-related topic.

description.en: According to the Talmud, from Adam to Noah humans practiced vegetarianism (tzimchonut). In the Jewish sources, God's eventual permission to eat meat is often seen as nothing more than an ethical compromise and Jewish law restricts the type and way that meat is eaten.

A *minyan* is a quorum of ten Jewish adults – in traditional Orthodox communities, ten males, and in more progressive communities, ten people – required to recite specific public prayers and for other religious purposes. The Talmud [derives](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.21b.5?lang=bi&namedEntity=jewish-people&namedEntityText=children%20of%20Israel&with=Lexicon&lang2=en) this concept from the story of the [spies](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/the-spies?sort=Relevance&tab=notable-sources) and [elsewhere](https://www.sefaria.org/Ketubot.7a.13?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) mentions the books of Ruth and Psalms as sources of the requirement for a *minyan* in particular circumstances.

description.en: Toward the beginning of the Torah, pregnancy and childbirth are mentioned as part of Eve's punishment for eating from the tree of knowledge: God tells her, "[In hardship shall you bear children.](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.3.16?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&with=Navigation&lang2=en)" Later biblical stories tell of [struggles to conceive](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/infertility?tab=admin) and [challenges](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.25.22?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=en&with=all&lang2=en) of pregnancy. Rabbinic texts [express wonder](https://www.sefaria.org/Vayikra_Rabbah.14.2?lang=bi) at the miraculous nature of pregnancy, analyze halakhic aspects of pregnancy, – like whether pregnant women should fast on Yom Kippur – and discuss [unique prayers for](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.60a.13?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) pregnancy.

description.en: Tu B'Av — the fifteenth of Av — is a minor holiday. Falling just six days after the fast day of Tisha B'Av, which commemorates the destruction of the Temples in Jerusalem, Tu B'Av is described in rabbinic literature as one of the happiest days for the Jewish people. In antiquity, women would go out in festive clothing to dance in vineyards on this day. Today, the holiday is often viewed as a celebration of love.

description.he: הפרשת חלה היא מצווה מהתורה להפריש מעיסת בצק הלחם חלק שניתן לכהן. כשאר תרומות ומעשרות זוהי מצווה שמקיימים בארץ ישראל. מצוות הפרשת חלה היא אחת משלוש המצוות המזוהות עם נשים מאחר שבעבר הנשים היו מופקדות על מלאכות הבית. כיום מקיימים מצווה זו על פי דברי סופרים ורבים מייחסים לה סגולה וברכה ואף מוסיפים לה תפילות ובקשות.

enBio.value: The Tosafists - Ba'alei HaTosafot - were members of a school of Torah and Talmudic interpretation which flourished in 12th and 13th century France and Germany. Their roots are in the work of Rashi – in fact Rashi's sons-in-law and grandsons are counted amongst the founders and most influential members of the school of Tosafot. Their comments on almost every tractate of the Talmud were collected, edited, augmented and passed on for generations, with certain collections gaining more prominence (depending on tractate and locale). Their approach is analytical, comparative and incisive, and many times takes a critical stance regarding Rashi's commentary. They were amongst the first French and German rabbis to quote extensively the Jerusalem Talmud and the Talmud commentary of Rabbenu Chananel (of North Africa). Other works also emerged from their school, most notably Machzor Vitri and the Torah commentary, Da'at Z'kenim.

description.en: The tosafists — *ba'alei hatosafot* — were members of a school of Torah and talmudic interpretation that flourished in 12th- and 13th-century France and Germany. Their roots are in the work of [Rashi](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/rashi?tab=popular-writing-of). Rashi's own sons-in-law and grandsons are counted among the founders and most influential tosafists. Their comments on almost every tractate of the Talmud were collected, edited, augmented, and passed on for generations. Their approach is analytical, comparative, and incisive. They also often take a critical stance regarding Rashi's commentary. They were amongst the first French and German rabbis to quote the Jerusalem Talmud extensively and the commentary of [Rabbenu Chananel](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/rabeinu-chananel) on the Babylonian Talmud. Other works also emerged from their school, notably Machzor Vitri and the Torah commentary, Da'at Zekenim.

description.en: In kabbalistic literature, *Ein Sof*, or the Infinite One, has two meanings. One is the initial stage of creation, what is referred to as the Creator’s intent for creation, before the first [constriction](/topics/constriction) ([*tzimtzum*](/topics/tzimtzum1)), when the light and vessel are infinite. That is, there is an infinite will to receive that draws into it infinite light. The other meaning of *Ein Sof* is a “relative” *Ein Sof*, which is the [*Keter*](/topics/keter1) of each [level](/topics/level) of reality, because in relation to the [levels](/topics/level) beneath it, [*Keter*](/topics/keter1) is regarded as absolute light, without vessel or limitation. Thus, for example, the world of [*Adam Kadmon*](/topics/adam-kadmon2) is defined as *Ein Sof* in relation to the worlds of [*Atzilut*](/topics/atzilut), [*Beria*](/topics/beria1), [*Yetzira*](/topics/yetzira1), and [*Asiya*](/topics/asiya2), because the world of [*Adam Kadmon*](/topics/adam-kadmon2) is the [*Keter*](/topics/keter1) [level](/topics/level) of the lower four worlds. Similarly, the [*partzuf*](/topics/partzuf1) called Atik (literally, “Ancient”), the highest [*partzuf*](/topics/partzuf1) of an individual world, is the [*Keter*](/topics/keter1) of its respective world, and is defined as *Ein Sof* in relation to that world. The same applies to the [*sefira*](/topics/sefira2) of [*Keter*](/topics/keter1) in each [*partzuf*](/topics/partzuf1): It is defined as *Ein Sof* relative to that [*partzuf*](/topics/partzuf1). The focus of most of the *Zohar* is on this relative *Ein Sof*.

description.en: The "three weeks" refers to a period from the fast of the [17th of Tammuz](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/shivah-asar-betammuz?tab=admin) until the fast of [Tisha B'Av](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/tisha-bav?sort=Relevance&tab=notable-sources). The period is considered one of mourning over the destruction of the Temples in Jerusalem and other calamities in Jewish history. In many communities, it is marked by mourning customs, such as avoiding weddings, events with live music, and haircuts.

description.en: The Red Sea (Yam Suf in Hebrew) — often mistranslated as the Reed Sea — is located along Egypt's eastern border. enBio.value: Ovadiah ben Ya'akov Seforno was an Italian rabbi, Biblical commentator, philosopher, halachic authority, and physician who wrote commentaries on a good portion of the Tanach. After an early period of wandering, he settled in Bologna, where he founded a yeshiva. Sforno was held in high regard by his contemporaries, Maharam Padua and Maharik Kolon  and is also quoted in responsa of contemporary authorities who consulted him on issues of Halacha. Seforno was admired for his wide knowledge by Henry II, King of France, to whom he sent a Latin translation he prepared of his philosophical work, Or Amim.

description.en: Many biblical characters display courage, like the midwives who defy Pharaoh's decree to kill Jewish babies or [Queen Esther](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/esther), who exposes the plan of the evil [Haman](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/haman) to King [Ahasuerus](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/ahasuerus). The charge to "[be strong and courageous](https://www.sefaria.org/Joshua.1.6?lang=bi&with=Translations&lang2=en)" appears several times throughout the Bible, especially to the character of Joshua as he prepares to lead the people into the land of Israel. Rambam, the 12th-century scholar, [counts](https://www.sefaria.org/Sefer_HaMitzvot%2C_Negative_Commandments.58.1?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) the prohibition of fearing the enemy and deserting battle as one of the commandments, and other rabbinic, Chasidic, and kabbalistic sources analyze the merits and qualities necessary to achieve courage.

description.en: The constriction refers to a diminishing of the divine light. This constriction does not constitute a change in the divine light itself, as the Creator bestows His light constantly and fully. Rather, any constriction of the light is the result of a change in the created vessels formed of the will to receive. In order for constriction to take place, the vessel is modified through the placement of a [partition](/topics/partition2) upon it so that it is prevented from receiving the light. There are two types of constriction in the process of creation, the first constriction (in which a [partition](/topics/partition2) is placed upon the vessel), and the [second constriction](/topics/second-constriction).
An appointed time.

Colors appear throughout the Tanakh as elements of ritual, status, and symbolism. The commandment of [ritual fringes](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/tzitzit?sort=Relevance&tab=admin), for example, includes the incorporation of *[tekhelet](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/tekhelet?sort=Relevance&tab=admin)*, a blueish dye. Descriptions of the Mishkan repeatedly emphasize the use of colored materials — blue, purple, and crimson wool — in its curtains and priestly garments. The Torah requires taking a [red heifer](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/parah-adumah?sort=Relevance&tab=admin) as part of the purification process for those who have come into contact with death, and a priest determines whether someone has *tzara'at* – a discoloration condition on skin, a house, or clothing – in part based on the color of the mark. Later Jewish texts elaborate on the detail and significance of color in these instances and more.

description.en: The Torah, Judaism's foundational text, begins with creative acts as God makes the world over six days. The same chapter describes how the first humans are created in [the image of God](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.1.27?lang=he&with=all&lang2=he) and tasked with the project of creating new life and filling the earth. Texts throughout the Jewish textual tradition speak of the importance of imbuing religious practice — from [prayer](https://www.sefaria.org/Psalms.96.1?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=he&with=all&lang2=he) to [Torah study](https://www.sefaria.org/Chagigah.3a.15?ven=hebrew|William_Davidson_Edition_-_Vocalized_Aramaic&lang=he&with=all&lang2=he) — with creative spirit, the nature of creative work and its prohibition on Shabbat, and ownership rights of those who create.
